Two hundred denarii was therefore well over half a year’s wages, which is the point of Philip’s reply."},{"verse":14,"phrase":"the Prophet","lemma":"προφήτης","kind":"background","traditional":"the Prophet","note":"The crowd is not calling Jesus one prophet among many. They identify him with the prophet like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18:15–18, a figure many expected in the last days. A feeding in a remote place near Passover would naturally recall Moses and the manna, and the move to make Jesus king in the next verse follows from that expectation."},{"verse":19,"phrase":"stadia","lemma":"στάδιον","kind":"background","traditional":"three or four miles; furlongs","note":"A stadion was a Greek measure of about 185 metres, so twenty-five or thirty stadia is roughly three to three and a half miles (about five kilometres). The lake is about seven miles across at its widest, so the disciples were well out from shore."},{"verse":20,"phrase":"It is I","lemma":"ἐγώ εἰμι","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"It is I","note":"The Greek is literally “I am”, which is the ordinary way to say “It’s me”, and that is the plain sense here. The same two words open “I am the bread of life” in verse 35 and stand alone at John 8:58, and in the Greek Old Testament they are used for God’s self-declaration (for example Isaiah 43:10). Many interpreters think John intends that echo in this scene of mastery over the sea, but this cannot be proved from the phrase alone."},{"verse":27,"phrase":"eternal life","lemma":"αἰώνιος","kind":"background","traditional":"eternal life; everlasting life","note":"The adjective is formed from the word for “age”. In Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as its unending length. In John this life is something the believer already has (verses 47 and 54) and not only a future hope."},{"verse":31,"phrase":"He gave them bread from heaven to eat","lemma":"","kind":"background","traditional":"He gave them bread from heaven to eat","note":"The wording is closest to Psalm 78:24, with echoes of Exodus 16:4 and 16:15. The crowd is challenging Jesus to match Moses, and some Jewish writings from around this period expected manna to be given again in the age to come. The rest of the discourse is in effect an exposition of this quotation."},{"verse":33,"phrase":"that which comes down from heaven","lemma":"καταβαίνω","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"he who comes down from heaven; that which comes down from heaven","note":"The Greek can mean either “that which comes down” (the bread) or “he who comes down” (a person), because “bread” is grammatically masculine. The crowd takes it in the first sense, as their request in verse 34 shows, and the translation follows them. Jesus makes the personal sense explicit in verse 35, and the double meaning is probably deliberate."},{"verse":41,"phrase":"grumble","lemma":"γογγύζω","kind":"background","traditional":"murmur; grumble; complain","note":"This verb and its close relatives are what the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel’s grumbling against Moses in the wilderness, including in the manna story (Exodus 16–17; Numbers 14). A reader who knew those Scriptures would hear the echo: the hearers who appeal to the manna are behaving like the generation that ate it."},{"verse":54,"phrase":"eats","lemma":"τρώγω","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"eats; feeds on","note":"From this verse to verse 58 the Greek uses a different verb for eating from the one in verses 49–53. In older Greek it meant to gnaw or munch, and some interpreters think John chose it to make the language more graphic. Others point out that John uses it as his ordinary present-tense verb for “eat” (also at 13:18), so that no change of meaning is intended. The translation follows the second view; the question is disputed."},{"verse":60,"phrase":"harsh","lemma":"σκληρός","kind":"departure","traditional":"This is a hard saying","note":"The Greek word means hard in the sense of rough, harsh or unpleasant, not hard to understand. The disciples’ complaint is that what Jesus has said is objectionable, and “hard” in modern English suggests it was merely puzzling. Most translations keep “hard”; some use “difficult”. The final words could also be read “Who can listen to him?”"},{"verse":61,"phrase":"make you stumble","lemma":"σκανδαλίζω","kind":"departure","traditional":"Does this offend you?","note":"The verb means to trip someone up, to cause them to fall, and in the New Testament usually to fall away from faith. “Offend” was accurate in older English but now suggests hurt feelings. The stronger sense fits the context, since in verse 66 many disciples do turn back. Some recent translations render it similarly, with “cause to stumble” or “take offense”."},{"verse":64,"phrase":"hand him over","lemma":"παραδίδωμι","kind":"departure","traditional":"betray him","note":"The verb means to hand over or deliver up. The New Testament uses the same word for the leaders handing Jesus to Pilate and Pilate handing him over to be crucified. Greek has a separate word for betrayal, which is not used here. Most translations render “betray” when Judas is the subject, and the treachery is real, but it comes from the context and not from this word."},{"verse":66,"phrase":"Because of this","lemma":"","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"From that time; After this","note":"The Greek phrase can mean either “from this time on” or “as a result of this”. Translations are divided between the two. Both fit the context, and the difference is slight, since the departure follows directly on what Jesus has just said."},{"verse":69,"phrase":"the Holy One of God","lemma":"ἅγιος","kind":"textual","traditional":"that Christ, the Son of the living God","note":"The earliest manuscripts read “the Holy One of God”. Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, have “the Christ, the Son of the living God”, which most scholars regard as a harmonisation with Peter’s confession in Matthew 16:16. Elsewhere in the Gospels this title is used of Jesus only by an unclean spirit (Mark 1:24; Luke 4:34)."}],"candidates":[{"lemma":"ἀμήν","rendering":"Truly, truly","verse":26,"reason":"Jesus’s formula occurs about a hundred times across the Gospels, doubled in John, and translators vary between “truly”, “very truly”, “amen” and “I assure you”; it needs one treatment."},{"lemma":"μένω","rendering":"remain","verse":27,"reason":"A key Johannine term (also 1 John) rendered variously “abide”, “remain”, “endure”, “stay”; readers lose the thread from 6:27 and 6:56 to John 15 if the English varies."},{"lemma":"σκανδαλίζω","rendering":"make stumble","verse":61,"reason":"Frequent in the Gospels and Paul, where the traditional “offend” now misleads and alternatives range from “cause to sin” to “fall away”; the noun σκάνδαλον should be decided with it."},{"lemma":"παραδίδωμι","rendering":"hand over","verse":64,"reason":"Used of Judas, the leaders, Pilate and God handing Jesus over; rendering it “betray” only for Judas hides a deliberate thread across the Gospels and Paul."},{"lemma":"σάρξ","rendering":"flesh","verse":51,"reason":"Ranges from the physical body to human nature in its weakness or its opposition to the Spirit; translations vary widely (flesh, body, sinful nature, human effort), and consistency between John and Paul matters."}]}

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this Jesus went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, that is, of Tiberias.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A large crowd was following him, because they saw the signs he was performing on the sick.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus went up the mountain, and there he sat down with his disciples.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the Passover, the festival of the Jews, was near.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when Jesus looked up and saw that a large crowd was coming toward him, he said to Philip,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Where are we to buy bread so that these people may eat?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he was going to do.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Philip answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Bread worth two hundred denarii would not be enough for each of them to get even a little.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are these among so many?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Have the people sit down.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now there was plenty of grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus took the loaves, and after giving thanks he distributed them to those who were seated, and likewise of the fish, as much as they wanted.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they were full, he said to his disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Gather up the leftover pieces, so that nothing is lost.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with pieces of the five barley loaves that were left over by those who had eaten.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the people saw the sign he had performed, they began to say,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This truly is the Prophet who is to come into the world.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Jesus, knowing that they were about to come and seize him to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: got into a boat, and started across the sea toward Capernaum. It had already grown dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the sea was being stirred up by a strong wind that was blowing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were afraid.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is I; do not be afraid.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they wanted to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land they were heading for.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day the crowd that had stayed on the other side of the sea saw that there had been no other boat there, only the one, and that Jesus had not boarded the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they got into the boats themselves and went to Capernaum, looking for Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi, when did you get here?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly, truly, I tell you, you are looking for me not because you saw signs but because you ate of the loaves and were satisfied.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that remains to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you; for on him the Father, God, has set his seal.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What are we to do, to work the works of God?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “This is the work of God: that you believe in the one he sent.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Then what sign do you perform, so that we may see it and believe you? What work do you do?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Our ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness, as it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly, truly, I tell you, it is not Moses who has given you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For the bread of God is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Sir, give us this bread always.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I told you that you have seen me and yet do not believe.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never throw out,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: because I have come down from heaven not to do my own will but the will of the one who sent me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And this is the will of the one who sent me: that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For this is the will of my Father: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise them up on the last day.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the Jews began to grumble about him because he had said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am the bread that came down from heaven,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How can he now say, ‘I have come down from heaven’?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Stop grumbling among yourselves.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws them, and I will raise them up on the last day.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: It is written in the prophets: ‘And they will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Not that anyone has seen the Father except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever believes has eternal life.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I am the bread of life.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Your ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that a person may eat of it and not die.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, they will live forever. And the bread that I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the Jews began to quarrel with one another, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in yourselves.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise them up on the last day.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Just as the living Father sent me and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will also live because of me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like what the ancestors ate, and they died. Whoever eats this bread will live forever.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said these things while teaching in the synagogue in Capernaum.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Many of his disciples, when they heard it, said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This is a harsh saying. Who can listen to it?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus, knowing within himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Does this make you stumble?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then what if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is of no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and are life.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But there are some among you who do not believe.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would hand him over.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “This is why I have told you that no one can come to me unless it has been granted to them by the Father.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Because of this many of his disciples turned back and no longer went about with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Jesus said to the Twelve,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Surely you do not want to go away as well?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simon Peter answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have words of eternal life,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and we have come to believe and to know that you are the Holy One of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Did I not choose you, the Twelve? Yet one of you is a devil.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was speaking of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot; for this man, one of the Twelve, was going to hand him over.

notes.traditional: two hundred denarii; two hundred pennyworth; half a year’s wages
notes.note: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s pay for a hired labourer. Two hundred denarii was therefore well over half a year’s wages, which is the point of Philip’s reply.

The crowd is not calling Jesus one prophet among many. They identify him with the prophet like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18:15–18, a figure many expected in the last days. A feeding in a remote place near Passover would naturally recall Moses and the manna, and the move to make Jesus king in the next verse follows from that expectation.

A stadion was a Greek measure of about 185 metres, so twenty-five or thirty stadia is roughly three to three and a half miles (about five kilometres). The lake is about seven miles across at its widest, so the disciples were well out from shore.

The Greek is literally “I am”, which is the ordinary way to say “It’s me”, and that is the plain sense here. The same two words open “I am the bread of life” in verse 35 and stand alone at John 8:58, and in the Greek Old Testament they are used for God’s self-declaration (for example Isaiah 43:10). Many interpreters think John intends that echo in this scene of mastery over the sea, but this cannot be proved from the phrase alone.

The adjective is formed from the word for “age”. In Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as its unending length. In John this life is something the believer already has (verses 47 and 54) and not only a future hope.

notes.phrase: He gave them bread from heaven to eat
notes.traditional: He gave them bread from heaven to eat
notes.note: The wording is closest to Psalm 78:24, with echoes of Exodus 16:4 and 16:15. The crowd is challenging Jesus to match Moses, and some Jewish writings from around this period expected manna to be given again in the age to come. The rest of the discourse is in effect an exposition of this quotation.

notes.phrase: that which comes down from heaven
notes.traditional: he who comes down from heaven; that which comes down from heaven
notes.note: The Greek can mean either “that which comes down” (the bread) or “he who comes down” (a person), because “bread” is grammatically masculine. The crowd takes it in the first sense, as their request in verse 34 shows, and the translation follows them. Jesus makes the personal sense explicit in verse 35, and the double meaning is probably deliberate.

This verb and its close relatives are what the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel’s grumbling against Moses in the wilderness, including in the manna story (Exodus 16–17; Numbers 14). A reader who knew those Scriptures would hear the echo: the hearers who appeal to the manna are behaving like the generation that ate it.

From this verse to verse 58 the Greek uses a different verb for eating from the one in verses 49–53. In older Greek it meant to gnaw or munch, and some interpreters think John chose it to make the language more graphic. Others point out that John uses it as his ordinary present-tense verb for “eat” (also at 13:18), so that no change of meaning is intended. The translation follows the second view; the question is disputed.

The Greek word means hard in the sense of rough, harsh or unpleasant, not hard to understand. The disciples’ complaint is that what Jesus has said is objectionable, and “hard” in modern English suggests it was merely puzzling. Most translations keep “hard”; some use “difficult”. The final words could also be read “Who can listen to him?”

The verb means to trip someone up, to cause them to fall, and in the New Testament usually to fall away from faith. “Offend” was accurate in older English but now suggests hurt feelings. The stronger sense fits the context, since in verse 66 many disciples do turn back. Some recent translations render it similarly, with “cause to stumble” or “take offense”.

The verb means to hand over or deliver up. The New Testament uses the same word for the leaders handing Jesus to Pilate and Pilate handing him over to be crucified. Greek has a separate word for betrayal, which is not used here. Most translations render “betray” when Judas is the subject, and the treachery is real, but it comes from the context and not from this word.

The Greek phrase can mean either “from this time on” or “as a result of this”. Translations are divided between the two. Both fit the context, and the difference is slight, since the departure follows directly on what Jesus has just said.

notes.traditional: that Christ, the Son of the living God
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts read “the Holy One of God”. Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, have “the Christ, the Son of the living God”, which most scholars regard as a harmonisation with Peter’s confession in Matthew 16:16. Elsewhere in the Gospels this title is used of Jesus only by an unclean spirit (Mark 1:24; Luke 4:34).

candidates.reason: Jesus’s formula occurs about a hundred times across the Gospels, doubled in John, and translators vary between “truly”, “very truly”, “amen” and “I assure you”; it needs one treatment.
A key Johannine term (also 1 John) rendered variously “abide”, “remain”, “endure”, “stay”; readers lose the thread from 6:27 and 6:56 to John 15 if the English varies.
Frequent in the Gospels and Paul, where the traditional “offend” now misleads and alternatives range from “cause to sin” to “fall away”; the noun σκάνδαλον should be decided with it.
Used of Judas, the leaders, Pilate and God handing Jesus over; rendering it “betray” only for Judas hides a deliberate thread across the Gospels and Paul.

Ranges from the physical body to human nature in its weakness or its opposition to the Spirit; translations vary widely (flesh, body, sinful nature, human effort), and consistency between John and Paul matters.
